The history of computing is often told as a story of hardware, of ever smaller and faster switches, but the more interesting thread runs through the ideas. Before there were transistors there were procedures, and before there were procedures there was the recognition that a mechanical process could stand in for a mental one. That recognition arrived slowly and from several directions at once. Mathematicians wanted to know which problems could be settled by rote, engineers wanted machines that would not tire, and logicians wanted to know what followed from what. The answers they found turned out to be the same answer.

Rivers do not simply run downhill; they negotiate. A river meeting soft ground will widen and slow, dropping the sediment it has carried from higher land, and over centuries that deposition builds the very floodplain through which the river then wanders. Meeting hard rock, the same river narrows and quickens, cutting downward rather than sideways. The shape of a valley is therefore a record of an argument between water and stone, conducted over a timescale that makes the outcome look inevitable when it was nothing of the kind.

Good documentation is not a description of what the code does. Anyone can read the code for that, and the code will always be more accurate than the prose beside it. Documentation earns its place by recording what the code does not say: why this approach was chosen over the obvious one, which constraint made the simple version unworkable, what was tried and abandoned. A comment that restates the line below it is worse than no comment, because it must be maintained and it will not be, and eventually it will lie.

The domestication of grasses is the least appreciated revolution in human history. Wheat, rice, maize and barley are all grasses, and all were reshaped by selection into forms that cannot reproduce without human help. The seed head of wild wheat shatters when ripe, scattering grain across the ground; the domesticated variety holds its seed until it is cut. That single change, useless to the plant and essential to the farmer, is what made harvest possible and therefore what made storage, surplus, and cities possible.

Measurement changes what it measures, and not only in physics. A metric that is merely observed will drift with the thing it tracks; a metric that is rewarded will be optimised directly, and the quantity it was chosen to represent will quietly detach from it. This is why the most useful indicators are often the ones nobody is accountable for. The moment a proxy becomes a target, it begins to decay as a proxy, and the decay is fastest where the incentive is strongest.

Sleep is not a single state but a cycle of several, and the ordering matters. Slow-wave sleep dominates the early part of the night and appears to be when declarative memory is consolidated; REM sleep grows longer towards morning and is associated with procedural and emotional processing. Waking someone repeatedly does not merely shorten sleep, it changes its composition, and a full night of fragmented sleep can leave a person more impaired than a shorter night left undisturbed.
